nodes.text: Let $n$ be a sufficiently large integer. Suppose $A\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ has $\lvert A\rvert=n$ and minimises the number of distinct distances between points in $A$. Prove that there are at least two (and probably many) such $A$ which are non-similar.

#91 : [Er87b,p.171] [Er90] [Er97e] geometry | distances For $n=3$ the equilateral triangle is the only such set. For $n=4$ the square or two equilateral triangles sharing an edge give two non-similar examples. For $n=5$ the regular pentagon is the unique such set (which has two distinct distances). Erdős mysteriously remarks in [Er90] this was proved by 'a colleague'. (In [Er87b] this is described as 'a colleague from Zagreb (unfortunately I do not have his letter)'.) A published proof of this fact is provided by Kovács [Ko24c] . In [Er87b] Erdős says that there are at least two non-similar examples for $6\leq n\leq 9$. The minimal possible number of distinct distances is the subject of [89] .
